title: Seventh Chords
description: Add a fourth note to a triad for richer colors: dominant 7th, major 7th and minor 7th chords.

steps.title: Adding a fourth note
steps.description:
A seventh chord is a triad with one more note stacked on top: the seventh. Which triad you start with, and which seventh you add, gives you three common flavors:

• Dominant 7th (C7): major triad + minor 7th. Bluesy, wants to move
• Major 7th (Cmaj7): major triad + major 7th. Smooth and dreamy
• Minor 7th (Cm7): minor triad + minor 7th. Warm and mellow

steps.title: Play C7
steps.description: Play C, E, G and Bb. Hear that slight edge? A dominant 7th sounds restless, like it wants to go somewhere. C7 especially wants to move to F major.
steps.hint: Bb is the black key just below B. Try thumb on C, then index, middle and pinky.

steps.title: Play Cmaj7
steps.description: Play C, E, G and B. Only one key is different from C7, but now it sounds soft and dreamy instead of restless.
steps.hint: Use B, the white key, not Bb. It sits right below the next C.

steps.title: Play Cm7
steps.description: Play C, Eb, G and Bb. Now both the third and the seventh are lowered, which gives the chord a warm, soulful sound.
steps.hint: Two black keys this time: Eb (between D and E) and Bb (between A and B).

steps.title: Play G7
steps.description: Play G, B, D and F. In the key of C, this is the dominant chord, the one that pulls hardest back to C.
steps.hint: All white keys. Skip one white key between each note.

steps.title: Tension and release
steps.description: A dominant 7th built on the fifth note of a key (V7) is full of tension, and that tension melts away when it moves to the home chord (I). Try G7, then C major, and listen for the release. V7 to I is one of the strongest pulls in music. You'll hear it closing countless classical pieces, hymns and pop songs.

steps.title: Which seventh?
steps.description: A major triad with a minor 7th on top. Which kind of seventh chord is that?
